note: Hunts are ranked by expected value to industry and humanity, weighed by how exactly a machine can verify them and how soon we can open them. Every hunt needs a judge program before it opens.

hunts.title: Vehicle routing benchmarks
hunts.why: Delivery, waste collection, ambulances: every percent saved on routes is fuel, money and CO2. Research groups still improve the best known solutions of the standard benchmark sets (CVRPLIB).
hunts.verify: Exact: the judge checks every customer is served once, capacities hold, and recomputes the total distance.

hunts.title: Job-shop scheduling (Taillard instances)
hunts.why: Factories, chip fabs, cloud clusters: shorter schedules mean more output from the same machines. Some classic benchmark instances still have open best-known makespans.
hunts.verify: Exact: the judge replays the schedule, checks machine and order constraints, and measures the makespan.

hunts.title: Fewer multiplications for matrix products
hunts.why: Matrix products are the heart of AI hardware. In 2025 AlphaEvolve found a 4x4 scheme with 48 multiplications; small-format records are still moving.
hunts.verify: Exact: the judge expands the proposed formula symbolically and checks it equals the matrix product for every entry.

hunts.title: Sorting networks
hunts.why: Fixed comparator circuits sort data on GPUs, FPGAs and in standard libraries. Fewer comparators or fewer layers mean faster, cheaper hardware; optimal sizes are unknown beyond small n.
hunts.verify: Exact: by the 0-1 principle the judge runs every 0/1 input (2^n of them) through the network.

hunts.title: Error-correcting codes
hunts.why: Phones, satellites, disks and QR codes rely on codes that fix errors. Tables of the largest known codes for given length and distance still have gaps.
hunts.verify: Exact: the judge checks the pairwise Hamming distance of every pair of codewords.

hunts.title: Repair open source, with tests
hunts.why: The software the world runs on is maintained by too few people. A swarm fixing real issues, each fix proven by tests, is the most useful hunt of all.
hunts.verify: By tests: visible and hidden tests, plus guards. This needs the full Kickswarm coordinator.

hunts.title: Formal proofs in Lean
hunts.why: Formalized mathematics makes knowledge machine-checked forever, and trains the reasoning tools of tomorrow. Mathlib and open problem lists have thousands of unformalized results.
hunts.verify: Exact: the Lean proof checker accepts the proof or does not.

hunts.title: Packing circles
hunts.why: Packing is cutting, logistics, antenna and material design. The best known packings are improved every week by researchers worldwide.
hunts.verify: Exact: decimal arithmetic, radius computed and rounded down.

hunts.title: Ramsey graphs
hunts.why: Lower bounds for Ramsey numbers come from explicit graphs. Many bounds are decades old, and improving one is a recognised result.
hunts.verify: Exact: the judge searches the proposed graph for a forbidden clique or independent set.

hunts.title: Thomson problem: charges on a sphere
hunts.why: Electrons on a sphere, virus shells, the layout of points for climate grids and antennas. Lowest-energy configurations for large n are still being improved.
hunts.verify: Numerical with a published tolerance: the judge computes the energy in high precision.

hunts.title: Low-discrepancy point sets
hunts.why: Better spread points make Monte Carlo simulations, finance, rendering and machine learning converge faster.
hunts.verify: Exact for small sets: the judge computes the star discrepancy.

hunts.title: No three in line
hunts.why: A century-old puzzle (Dudeney, 1917). Perfect solutions are known up to n = 60; beyond that, nobody has published one.
hunts.verify: Exact: integer arithmetic over every triple of points.
